messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Linh is a 22-year-old Vietnamese-American woman who works as a call center agent and has been married for just over a year. She presented for intake with a PCL-5 score of 61, describing a presentation that has steadily worsened over the past eighteen months following a sexual assault perpetrated by a male supervisor at a previous job. The assault occurred in a back office after a shift; he had called her in under the guise of a performance review. What she remembers of that evening does not arrive as a continuous story — it comes in disconnected pieces that refuse to assemble: the texture of the chair, a particular taste she cannot name but cannot escape, the sound of a door locking. These fragments feel more immediate to her than anything she has experienced since, more real than her wedding day, more vivid than her husband's face at breakfast. She has described them as intrusions that arrive without warning rather than memories she can choose to revisit.

The assault happened in a context saturated with authority, and that saturation has spread outward into her daily life. When Linh encounters anyone in a position of power — a floor supervisor at the call center walking the aisles, a security guard in a parking structure — her body responds before her mind can intervene. She has developed a habit of scanning every room she enters for exits, a reflex so automatic she now does it in her own home. Unexpected movement nearby — a colleague leaning across her desk, her husband reaching past her — triggers a startle response she cannot suppress. She had come to believe that vigilance is the only thing standing between her and another assault; to let her guard down, even briefly, felt to her like an invitation.

The call center environment has become one of the most difficult spaces in her life to navigate. Male supervisors are a constant presence, and the open floor plan offers no clear escape. On days when a manager stops near her station, the fragmented memories surface with particular force — the taste returning first, then the physical sense of confinement — and Linh finds herself scanning the room for the nearest door while still speaking to a customer. These intrusions, arriving unbidden and feeling more real than the present moment, drive her toward the strategies she has come to rely on: she deflects any conversation that edges toward the assault, refuses to acknowledge it when her husband or a coworker inadvertently references something adjacent to it, and has increasingly used sexual fantasy as a way of reclaiming a sense of control over her own body. She understood, on some level, that this last strategy was not resolution — but it temporarily quieted what nothing else could.

What Linh had come to believe about herself was perhaps the most corrosive part of her presentation. She was certain she was inadequate — that her inability to simply move forward proved something fundamental about her character. This appraisal of herself as broken kept her from disclosing the full extent of her symptoms to her husband, which in turn kept her isolated in the very relationship that might have offered repair. She was equally certain that thinking directly about the event would undo her entirely — that if she allowed the memories to surface fully rather than in pieces, she would not survive the experience. This conviction made the fragmented quality of the memories feel like protection, and so she never tried to integrate them, which meant they remained raw and trigger-ready. Her belief that she must be on guard at all times fed directly into her hypervigilant scanning and her startle responses, and those bodily reactions, arriving in public and at work, confirmed for her that the danger was real and ongoing — that her vigilance was justified.

The avoidance had its own costs. By keeping the memories at arm's length, Linh found they grew no smaller; the fragmented pieces continued to surface in response to an ever-widening range of cues. A family gathering — her husband's relatives laughing together, children running between adults — could bring on a wave of shame and grief she could not account for to anyone present. An ambulance passing the call center window was enough to tighten the loop entirely. What finally brought her to seek help was a performance review scheduled by a new female supervisor — a routine meeting — during which Linh had a panic response so severe she had to leave the building. She sat in her car for forty minutes before she could drive. What she most fears is that she will never feel safe in an ordinary room. What she most hopes, though she said it quietly and without much conviction, is that the pieces might someday fit together into something she can live with.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers (reminders/cues) directly lead to or produce negative appraisals/beliefs in Linh; the vignette shows triggers surfacing memories and driving avoidance strategies, but the causal link from triggers to negative appraisals is not established.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Linh's negative appraisals (e.g., believing she is broken, that thinking about the event will undo her) directly lead to or generate new triggers or triggering stimuli; the direction from appraisals back to triggers is not described.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that Linh's sense of threat or perceived danger directly leads to or drives her maladaptive strategies (deflection, avoidance, fantasy); the vignette links threat to hypervigilant scanning and startle but does not causally connect it to her avoidance/coping strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Linh's maladaptive strategies (avoidance, deflection, fantasy) directly lead to or create new triggers or an expanded range of triggering cues; while the vignette notes that avoidance kept memories 'trigger-ready' and that cues widened, it does not explicitly frame the strategies themselves as causing the triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She has developed a habit of scanning every room she enters for exits, a reflex so automatic she now does it in her own home. Unexpected movement nearby — a colleague leaning across her desk, her husband reaching past her — triggers a startle response she cannot suppress. She had come to believe that vigilance is the only thing standing between her and another assault; to let her guard down, even briefly, felt to her like an invitation.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And each time a trigger arrived — the floor supervisor's footsteps, the sound of a door clicking shut — it did not merely surface the memory; it delivered a verdict. In those moments Linh became certain, all over again, that she was permanently damaged, that ordinary life was not something she would ever be allowed to inhabit without terror.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What Linh had come to believe about herself was perhaps the most corrosive part of her presentation. She was certain she was inadequate — that her inability to simply move forward proved something fundamental about her character.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That conviction, once settled, did not stay contained to her self-image — it bled outward into how she read the world. Having concluded she was broken and that danger was permanent, she moved through ordinary days as though they were mined: a colleague's neutral glance, a shift in tone on a call, the particular way a door swung open — things she would once have registered and dismissed — now snagged and held her attention as potential signals, multiplying the range of cues that could set her off.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She had come to believe that vigilance is the only thing standing between her and another assault; to let her guard down, even briefly, felt to her like an invitation.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
It was this sustained sense of threat — the body-level certainty that harm was close and that she alone had to prevent it — that drove her toward the strategies she had assembled to survive: deflecting any conversation that edged near the assault, refusing to acknowledge adjacent references, and using sexual fantasy as a way of asserting some ownership over her own body. When the threat felt this immediate, those strategies were not avoidance in any abstract sense — they were the only architecture she had found that kept her functional.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
By keeping the memories at arm's length, Linh found they grew no smaller; the fragmented pieces continued to surface in response to an ever-widening range of cues.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The strategies themselves had drawn the map of the event around her: every deflection, every conversation cut short, every room she mentally exited before she had to leave it physically became its own daily marker of what had happened, and each marker was a new potential trigger. The avoidance had grown in all directions until whole categories of ordinary experience — a performance review, a closed-door meeting, a male voice adopting a particular register — carried the charge of the original harm, not despite her efforts to contain them but partly because of them.
<<<END>>>
